shang-dynasty: The earliest historically confirmed Chinese dynasty, ruling the fertile Yellow River valley from capitals like Anyang (Yinxu) between c. 1600 and 1046 BCE. Renowned for masterful piece-mold ritual bronze casting, horse-drawn chariot warfare, and the earliest surviving Chinese writing inscribed on divination oracle bones.
zhou-dynasty: The longest-lasting dynasty in Chinese history (1046–256 BCE), which overthrew the Shang and established the political doctrine of the 'Mandate of Heaven'. Initially ruling through a decentralized feudal network of kinship fiefs (fengjian), the Western Zhou fostered classical Chinese cultural, ritual, and philosophical foundations.
cai: An ancient Chinese vassal state founded in the 11th century BCE by a younger brother of King Wu of Zhou in modern Henan. Positioned precariously between the central plains and the expanding southern power of Chu, Cai survived centuries of border conflicts through shifting alliances before final annexation by Chu in 447 BCE.
cao: A regional vassal state of the Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn periods, established in the 11th century BCE in modern western Shandong. Governed by descendants of King Wen of Zhou from their capital at Taoqiu, Cao prospered as an agricultural trade hub before being conquered by the neighboring State of Song in 487 BCE.
chen: An ancient Zhou vassal state situated in modern eastern Henan, traditionally founded by Duke Hu as descendants of the legendary sage-king Shun. Serving as a cultural buffer between northern Zhou states and the southern realm of Chu, Chen maintained distinctive shamanic religious traditions until its absorption by Chu in 478 BCE.
chu: A major southern powerhouse along the Yangtze and Han river valleys during the Zhou dynasty, with its capital at Ying in modern Hubei. Developing a rich, distinct culture characterized by elaborate bronze metallurgy, lacquerware, and Daoist poetic traditions, Chu expanded aggressively to become one of the most formidable Seven Warring States.
jin: The dominant northern super-state of the Spring and Autumn period, occupying modern Shanxi and northern Henan. Under Duke Wen of Jin, the state served as hegemon (ba) defending the central Zhou states against southern Chu expansion, until internal clan rivalries famously partitioned Jin into Han, Zhao, and Wei in 403 BCE.
later-zhou: The Eastern Zhou dynasty (770–256 BCE), established when King Ping moved the royal capital east to Luoyang following nomadic Rong raids that destroyed the western capital. Though royal power declined to nominal ceremonial status, this era witnessed immense intellectual flowering during the Hundred Schools of Thought, including Confucianism and Daoism.
lu: An influential Zhou vassal state in modern Shandong, founded by Boqin, the son of the revered Duke of Zhou. Celebrated as the cultural heartland of classical ritual, historical chronicle keeping, and moral philosophy, Lu was the birthplace of Confucius, preserving ancient Zhou rites long after other states had abandoned them.
qi: A wealthy and powerful maritime state in modern Shandong, founded in the 11th century BCE for the grand strategist Jiang Ziya. Blessed with rich coastal sea salt and silk industries, Qi established early hegemony under Duke Huan and prime minister Guan Zhong, later founding the renowned Jixia Academy of scholarly debate.
qin: A rugged frontier state in the western Wei River valley of modern Shaanxi, traditionally tasked with breeding warhorses and defending Zhou frontiers against nomadic tribes. Implementing radical Legalist reforms under Shang Yang, Qin developed a meritocratic military and centralized bureaucracy that ultimately conquered all rival states to unify China in 221 BCE.
song: An ancient central plains state in modern eastern Henan, granted by the Zhou kings to the surviving royal nobility of the defeated Shang dynasty to maintain ancestral rites. Famed for its merchant commerce and ethical adherence to ancient chivalric codes, Song was satirized in philosophical fables before being partitioned by Qi, Chu, and Wei.
teng: A minor aristocratic vassal state situated in modern southern Shandong during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. Despite its modest territory and vulnerability to powerful neighbors, Teng was celebrated by the philosopher Mencius as a model virtuous kingdom that governed through benevolence and classical rites before conquest by Song.
wey: A resilient central plains state along the Yellow River in modern northern Henan, founded by Kangshu, a younger brother of King Wu of Zhou. Renowned for poetry preserved in the Book of Songs and commercial craftsmanship, Wey survived as a small buffer state longer than any other, persisting until Qin annexation in 209 BCE.
wu: A dynamic maritime and riverine kingdom in the lower Yangtze delta of modern Jiangsu, centered around modern Suzhou. Expanding rapidly in the late Spring and Autumn period with the strategic advice of Sun Tzu, Wu dominated regional waterways with specialized navies and prized cast-bronze swords before being conquered by neighboring Yue in 473 BCE.
xu: An ancient non-Zhou Huaiyi confederation and state based along the Huai River valley in modern Anhui and Jiangsu. Under charismatic rulers like King Yan of Xu, the state challenged Western Zhou supremacy and spread distinctive southeastern bronze culture before being conquered by the expanding state of Wu in 512 BCE.
yan: A major northeastern frontier kingdom centered at modern Beijing, established at the start of the Western Zhou dynasty by the Duke of Shao. Guarding the northern borders against Steppe nomads and trading with Manchuria and Korea, Yan constructed extensive early walls and endured as one of the Seven Warring States until Qin conquest.
zheng: An influential central plains vassal state founded in the late Western Zhou in modern Henan, centered on the commercial capital of Xinzheng. Under the astute leadership of Duke Zhuang, Zheng was the first state to challenge royal Zhou authority, pioneering the interstate balance of power during the early Spring and Autumn period.
zhu: A minor regional state in modern southwestern Shandong ruled by the Cao lineage, also known historically as Zhulou or Zou. Located near the cultural heartland of Lu, the state maintained close ties to Confucian traditions and is celebrated as the ancestral birthplace of the influential philosopher Mencius before annexation by Chu.
yue: An ancient indigenous kingdom centered south of the Yangtze River around modern Zhejiang and northern Fujian, famed for seafaring, aquaculture, and peerless bronze sword metallurgy. Under King Goujian, Yue rebounded from near destruction to conquer its bitter northern rival Wu in 473 BCE, briefly achieving hegemony before succumbing to Chu.
han: One of the Seven Warring States, established in 403 BCE when three noble families partitioned the great state of Jin in modern Henan and Shanxi. Positioned strategically in the central plains, Han was an advanced center of iron weaponry and crossbow manufacture, but its small size left it vulnerable to conquest by neighboring Qin in 230 BCE.
wei: One of the Seven Warring States created from the partition of Jin, occupying the fertile central Yellow River plains of modern Shanxi and Henan. Under Marquis Wen and the Legalist reforms of Li Kui, Wei became the premier military and economic superpower of the early Warring States before facing defeats against Qin and Qi.
zhao: A powerful northern kingdom among the Seven Warring States, formed from the partition of Jin in modern Shanxi and Hebei. Under King Wuling, Zhao revolutionized Chinese warfare by adopting nomadic cavalry tactics and clothing ('Hu clothing and mounted archery'), defending northern frontiers against Steppe nomads until crushed by Qin at the catastrophic Battle of Changping.
zhongshan: A unique kingdom in the central plains of modern Hebei, founded by the semi-nomadic White Di (Baidi) pastoralists during the Warring States period. Remarkably synthesizing Steppe nomadic traditions with sophisticated Zhou ritual culture and bronze casting, Zhongshan built fortified capitals and resisted Zhao and Wei invasions for over a century before falling in 296 BCE.
yuezhi: An ancient Indo-European pastoral nomadic confederation that originally dominated the grasslands and oasis corridors of the Hexi Corridor in modern Gansu. Driven westward across Central Asia after defeats by the Xiongnu, the Yuezhi conquered Greco-Bactria and eventually settled in northern India to establish the magnificent Kushan Empire.
xiongnu: A formidable pastoral nomadic confederation that unified the Mongolian steppe under Modu Chanyu in the late 3rd century BCE. Fielding hundreds of thousands of horse archers, the Xiongnu built the first great nomadic empire in Inner Asia, extracting trade and tribute from Han China and prompting the construction of the Great Wall.
